meaning: Enmity toward God and the consequence of sin – humanity's rebellion and judgment
description: The number 36 appears in the Bible most notably in Joshua 7:5, where exactly 36 Israelites fell at Ai as a direct consequence of Achan’s sin and disobedience to God. This event illustrates how one person’s rebellion can have fatal consequences for the entire community. As the product of 6×6, the number can be linked to an intensification of the number 6, which symbolizes human weakness and insufficiency without God – here doubly emphasized. The number also occurs in 2 Chronicles 16:1, where it marks Asa’s 36th year of reign, a turning point when Baasha of Israel threatened Judah – a context marked by political conflict and failing trust in God.

versions.meaning: Enmity toward God and the consequence of sin – linked to humanity's rebellion and judgment, as a product of 6×6.
versions.description: The number 36 appears in the Bible most notably in Joshua 7:5, where exactly 36 Israelites fell at Ai as a direct consequence of Achan's sin and disobedience to God. As the product of 6×6, the number can be linked to an intensification of the number 6, which symbolizes human weakness and insufficiency without God. In Jewish tradition outside the Bible (Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b and Sukkah 45b), there is the teaching about 36 hidden righteous ones (Lamed-Vav Tzadikim) who sustain the world, and the number 36 is double 18, which has the numerical value (gematria) of the Hebrew word 'chai' (life). This tradition is however post-biblical and belongs to rabbinic/mystical Judaism rather than the Bible's own symbolism.

footnotes.text: In Jewish tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b and Sukkah 45b) there is the teaching about the 36 hidden righteous ones (Lamed-Vav Tzadikim) who sustain the world. This tradition is post-biblical and belongs to rabbinic/mystical Judaism rather than the Bible's own symbolism.
The number 36 is double 18, which has the numerical value (gematria) of the Hebrew word 'chai' (חי), meaning 'life'. This connection is central in Jewish numerology and gift-giving practices.
